rv.q: That may be why the lightness of the National Theater’s modern-dress “Hamlet,” on tour at the Brooklyn Academy of Music, is so discordant.
For a few halfhearted laughs they sacrifice the ability to make us care.
This contemporary Hamlet succeeds in making a four-hundred-year-old tragedy feel urgent, accessible, and vibrantly connected to the anxieties of the present moment.
In those respects, certainly, this “Hamlet” succeeds.
Hiran Abeysekera pulls out a charmingly cheeky yet heartbreakingly boyish Danish prince in Robert Hastie’s production of Hamlet from the National Theatre.
So this is a mixed Hamlet but even an uneven production of the world’s greatest play brings rewards and is worth your time.
Unpersuasive as this Hamlet may ultimately be, there are only great things fated for Francesca Mills after this intrepid performance of Ophelia.
This “Hamlet” is often amusing, sometimes hilariously so, but it is rarely tragic.
Of course, Hamlet remains fascinating all by its 426-year-old self and as somebody remarks, the play’s the thing, and the National Theatre capably serves it here.
And that is certainly the greatest asset of the new Hamlet from the UK’s National Theatre, presently on loan at Brooklyn Academy of Music’s (BAM) Harvey Theater.

With a strong respect for the text, a clear vision from Director Robert Hastie , and restrained use of stage effects, this Hamlet is a fine addition to the finest renditions of the play, offering an intimate portrayal of the prince and his most private perceptions.
The ensemble is a wonderfully sharpened group of theater artists.
Individual moments register, but they don’t always connect.

cn.t: This National Theatre production earns mixed reviews for its modern approach and Hiran Abeysekera's unconventional, polarizing performance, with critics praising Francesca Mills' standout Ophelia but questioning the show's overall coherence.
